record.paper_title: Open Problems within Nonextensive Statistical Mechanics
record.original_question: For the q-Fourier transform in NSM, can its current limitations be validated as physically meaningful limits in applications involving heavy-tailed distributions, or can a symmetric generalized Fourier transform be defined instead? In particular, can one define a mathematically rigorous mapping between compact-support and heavy-tailed domains, so that a transform mapping q-Gaussians between those domains qualifies as a genuine generalized Fourier transform for complex signals?

evidence.quote: Open Problem 5: As currently defined, the q-Fourier transform of NSM has limited physical applications, since a) the inverse is not symmetric and b) the image function has slower decaying tails. Can these limitations be validated by limits within physical applications of heavy-tailed distributions or can a symmetric generalization of the Fourier transform be defined?

A candidate for a symmetric Fourier transform maps q-Gaussians between their heavy-tailed and compact-support domains but currently lacks a general mapping between these domains. Can a mathematically rigorous mapping between the compact-support and heavy-tailed domains be defined that would qualify as a generalization of the Fourier transform?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
For a real parameter $q$, define the $q$-exponential $e_q(x) = [1+(1-q)x]_+^{1/(1-q)}$ (with $e_1(x)=e^x$), and the $q$-Gaussian probability density $G_q(\beta;x) = A_q \sqrt{\beta}\, e_q(-\beta x^2)$, normalized to unit mass. For $q<1$, $G_q$ has compact support $|x|\le 1/\sqrt{(1-q)\beta}$; for $1<q<3$, $G_q$ has heavy (power-law) tails. The $q$-Fourier transform is defined, for $1\le q<3$ and suitable nonnegative $f$, by
$$F_q[f](\xi) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e_q\!\bigl(i\xi\, x\, [f(x)]^{q-1}\bigr)\, f(x)\, dx,$$
and it maps $q$-Gaussians to $q'$-Gaussians for an explicit $q'=q'(q)$. This transform is known to suffer from two limitations: (i) its inverse is not symmetric (it is not an involution up to reflection), and (ii) the image of a $q$-Gaussian with $1<q<3$ is a $q'$-Gaussian whose tails decay more slowly than those of the original.

Address the following questions.

1. Determine whether these two limitations can be interpreted as physically meaningful constraints inherent to transforms acting on heavy-tailed distributions, in the sense that no symmetric (involutive) integral transform can preserve the class of heavy-tailed $q$-Gaussians and respect the $q\leftrightarrow q'$ duality.

2. Alternatively, construct a symmetric (involutive up to reflection) generalized Fourier transform $\mathcal{F}$ on an appropriate function space containing all $q$-Gaussians for $q\in(-\infty,3)$, such that $\mathcal{F}$ reduces to the standard Fourier transform when $q=1$ and maps $q$-Gaussians to $q$-Gaussians (or to a symmetric counterpart).

3. In particular, construct a mathematically rigorous bijective mapping between the compact-support domain $q<1$ and the heavy-tailed domain $1<q<3$ such that, under this mapping, a $q$-Gaussian on one side corresponds to a $q$-Gaussian on the other, and verify that the resulting transform satisfies the defining properties (linearity on the relevant space, an inversion formula, and reduction to the classical Fourier transform at $q=1$) qualifying it as a genuine generalization of the Fourier transform suitable for complex-valued signals.
artifact.status_search_result: The asymmetry and tail-broadening features of the $q$-Fourier transform have been analyzed in the literature (e.g., reflections on the $q$-Fourier transform and $q$-Gaussian function, and Fourier analysis of $q$-Gaussians), and partial frameworks (tempered ultradistributions, alternative characterizations) have been proposed. However, no published construction is currently recognized as a fully symmetric generalized Fourier transform with a rigorous bijection between compact-support and heavy-tailed $q$-Gaussian domains, so the problem appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Reflections on the q-Fourier transform and the q-Gaussian function
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses limitations and properties of the q-Fourier transform and its action on q-Gaussian functions.
status_evidence.claim: The asymmetry/non-involutive nature of the q-Fourier transform is acknowledged and analyzed but not resolved by a symmetric generalization.

status_evidence.title: Fourier Analysis and q-Gaussian Functions: Analytical and Numerical Results
status_evidence.snippet: Theoretical and numerical study of Fourier transforms of q-Gaussians, including compact-support and heavy-tailed regimes.
status_evidence.claim: Existing analyses provide partial results but do not establish a rigorous symmetric mapping between compact-support and heavy-tailed q-Gaussian domains.
